title: Jogless stripes in the round
subtitle: Eliminating the colour jog where a new stripe begins in circular knitting.
excerpt: When knitting stripes in the round, the colour change always produces a visible step or jog at the start of the round. The jogless method lifts the last stitch of the previous round over the first stitch of the new colour to close the gap, producing a smooth, continuous stripe.
sourceNotes: Jogless stripe technique widely documented in UK and US knitting publications. The slip-stitch variant is credited in multiple modern knitting references as standard practice for circular stripe work.
heroPrompt: Close-up of even, seamless horizontal stripes in two colours on a circular knitted hat, showing no visible jog at the colour change point.

glossaryTerms.definition: The small visible step that appears at the start of each round when working stripes in the round, caused by knitting in a spiral rather than a true circle.

content.text: Circular knitting works in a continuous spiral, which means every round starts one stitch to the left of the round before. When you change colour, this spiral produces a

at the round marker, a half-stitch step where the two colours meet. The jogless technique corrects this by slipping the first stitch of the second round of the new colour purlwise, effectively lifting the previous round's colour up to cover the gap. It suits any simple stripe worked in stocking stitch in the round. Difficulty: intermediate.
DK or aran weight yarn in two or more colours
A circular needle or DPNs in the appropriate size for your yarn
Knit the last round of colour A as normal up to and including the stitch before the marker.
Slip the marker. Join colour B and knit the entire first round of colour B, working past the marker and continuing around.

At the start of the second round of colour B, slip the marker and then slip the first stitch of the round purlwise (with yarn in back). This is the key move: it draws the colour A stitch up on the right side, closing the jog.
Continue knitting the rest of the second round normally in colour B.
Repeat the sequence for each subsequent colour change: knit the full first round of the new colour, then slip the first stitch of the second round purlwise.

attrs.title: Stripes wider than two rounds
attrs.body: The slip only needs to happen at the first round of each new colour. If your stripe is four or more rounds deep, slip the first stitch on the second round of each colour change and knit all remaining rounds of that stripe normally.

content.text: Jogless stripes appear in hats, socks, and yoked sweaters where two or more colours alternate in horizontal rounds. The technique works best on stripes of two rounds or more. Single-round stripes are better handled with helical knitting, which avoids the jog by working both colours in a spiral.

items.symptom: A small ladder or loose stitch appears at the slip point
items.cause: The slipped stitch was worked too loosely
items.fix: Slip the stitch snugly and continue into the next stitch without pausing. The slip should feel firm against the needle.

items.symptom: The jog is still visible even after slipping
items.cause: The first stitch of the new colour was knitted rather than slipped on the second round
items.fix: Check the sequence. The correction happens on round two of the new colour, not round one. If the stitch was knitted, the jog remains.

items.symptom: The slip distorts the fabric in a different place
items.cause: The round marker was moved or the slip was placed one stitch too early or late
items.fix: Work the slip on the very first stitch after the round marker at the start of the second round of the new colour.
